newsitem.title: USA: SWIMMING-RUSSIAN-BORN KRAYZELBURG SETS U.S. MARK AT NATIONALS.
newsitem.headline: SWIMMING-RUSSIAN-BORN KRAYZELBURG SETS U.S. MARK AT NATIONALS.

text.p: Russian-born Lenny Krayzelburg broke his adopted country's record in the 200-meter backstroke with the fastest time in the world this year at the U.S. Swimming Nationals Friday night.
Krayzelburg, 21, who became a U.S. citizen in 1995, was just two hundredths of a second off Olympian Tripp Schwenk's U.S. record of one minute and 58.35 seconds in the morning preliminary.
He broke the mark in the championship final with a time of 1:58.04. "My coach told me I had an American record in me," said Krayzelburg, who was born in Odessa, Russia.
Olympic gold medalist Brad Bridgewater, Krayzelburg's training partner, was second in 1:59.40.
Krayzelburg, who was on pace to break Spaniard Martin Zubero's world mark of 1:56.57 for the first 100 meters, earned a spot on the U.S. world championships team.
This meet served as U.S. team trials for the world championships, Pan Pacific Championships and World University Games.
"It is very satisfying being a U.S. citizen winning a national title, and even more satisfying beating the American record holder," Krayzelburg said of Schwenk, who finished fifth in 2:02.61.
"The newest American set the American record," U.S. men's world team coach John Urbanchek said. "We were very proud of that."
Amy Van Dyken, who walked away from the Atlanta Games with four gold medals, won the women's 50-meter freestyle in 25.10 seconds just one month after resuming training.
Van Dyken, who was also fastest in morning qualifying, won Olympic gold last summer in the 50 freestyle, 100 butterfly, 400 freestyle relay and 400 medley relay.
Chad Carvin, who missed the 1996 Olympic trials with cardiomyopathy -- a virus that attacks the heart muscle -- won the 1,500-meter freestyle in 15:15.63.
Carvin added the 1,500 title to the 400-meter gold he won earlier in the week here.

In the night's other final, 18-year-old Misty Hyman won the women's 200-meter butterfly in 2:09.08 to sweep the butterfly events. Hyman, who used her unique underwater start and fish kick to great effect, won the 100 butterfly title earlier in the week.
Overall, the seventh and final night of the meet turned up the fastest times of the week. But Urbanchek was not ready to assess his team's chances for the worlds in Perth, Australia next January.
"Since the rest of the world hasn't had a major meet, it's hard for us to judge where we stand," Urbanchek said.
"The rest of the world may equal what we have done here this week."
